title: asyncio queues: who goes next
intro: The queue classes from Python's standard library (asyncio/queues.py): Queue, PriorityQueue and LifoQueue, for passing items between coroutines. This is the real file with one line changed, apart from its imports. Start with put(), get() and _wakeup_next().

brief.purpose: asyncio.Queue is how coroutines in one Python process hand work to each other: producers put items in, consumers take them out, and either side can wait when the queue is full or empty. Crawlers, log processors and job runners are built on it.
constraints: Items must come out in the order they went in (first in, first out); PriorityQueue and LifoQueue change that rule on purpose.
Producers are often faster than consumers, so a queue can be given a maximum size, and put() then waits until there is room.
Many producers and consumers can wait on the same queue at once.
A waiting task can be cancelled at any moment, even right after it has been woken up.
Everything runs on one event-loop thread: no locks are needed, but a task can lose its turn at every await.

questions.text: q = Queue(maxsize=2). You call put_nowait('a'), put_nowait('b'), put_nowait('c'), then get_nowait() three times. What does each of the six calls do or return?

hints.text: full() compares qsize() with maxsize, and the _nowait methods raise instead of waiting.

questions.text: A PriorityQueue receives put_nowait((2, 'report')), put_nowait((1, 'page')), put_nowait((3, 'cleanup')) and put_nowait((1, 'alert')), in that order. In what order does get_nowait() return them, and why does 'alert' come out before 'page'?

hints.text: A PriorityQueue is a heap of tuples. How does Python compare two tuples whose first elements are equal?

questions.text: A consumer calls await q.get() on an empty queue. What is it waiting on, and what happens, step by step, when a producer then calls put_nowait('x')?

hints.text: A waiting get() sleeps on a future. Find the method put_nowait() calls to wake a sleeper.

questions.text: Read the bug report. Find the cause in the code, explain how it leads to what was observed and when it happens, and point to the lines with a code comment.

report.title: Sensor readings come out of order when the pipeline is busy
report.context: We feed sensor readings into an asyncio Queue with a maximum size, and one consumer task drains it. When the consumer falls behind and the queue fills up, readings come out in the wrong order; when traffic is light everything is in order. Reproduced with a queue of size 1 and four messages.
steps: Create Queue(maxsize=1) and put 'm1', so the queue is full.
Start three producer tasks that put 'm2', 'm3' and 'm4', in that order; each one has to wait for room.
Have one consumer get four messages.

hints.text: Once a message is inside the queue it keeps its place; look at what decides which waiting producer is let in next.
Read _wakeup_next() and ask which end of the waiters deque it takes from.

questions.text: After put() is woken up it checks full() again, in a while loop rather than an if. Why?

hints.text: Between being woken and running again, other tasks get a turn. What could they do to the queue?

questions.text: Why does the queue let you set a maxsize at all? What would happen in a pipeline whose producers are faster than its consumer if the queue were unbounded?

hints.text: Think about what put() does when the queue is full, and what happens to memory if it never has to.

questions.text: This section works, but it gets slower as the queue grows. Explain why and when that matters, and rewrite it.

hints.text: heapq.heappush keeps the list a heap in O(log n). What does sort() do on every put?

questions.text: How would you make a PriorityQueue keep arrival order among items that have the same priority?

hints.text: What could you put in the tuple between the priority and the item?
